extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Manual of Patent Examining Procedure guidance for making and documenting rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101, 102/103(b), and 112 (first and second paragraphs), and related procedural handling (e.g., Atomic Energy Act). Targeted at examiners conducting substantive examination of patent applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) precludes a rejection of process claims which involve the use or making of certain nonobvious biotechnological compositions of matter under 35 U.S.C. 103(a). 35 U.S.C. 103(b) requires that: (A) the biotechnological process and composition of matter be contained in either the same application or in separate applications having the same effective filing date; (B) both the biotechnological process and composition of matter be owned or subject to an assignment to the same person at the time the process was invented; (C) a patent issued on the process also contain the claims to the composition of matter used in or made by the process, or, if the process and composition of matter are in different patents, the patents expire on the same date; (D) the biotechnological process falls within the definition set forth in 35 U.S.C. 103(b); and (E) a timely election be made to proceed under the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 103(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An election is made by petition under 37 CFR 1.182 and must establish satisfaction of the statutory requirements. An election is normally timely if made no later than the earlier of payment of the issue fee or filing of an appeal brief in an application containing an un-rejected composition claim. For certain pending applications, timeliness may be satisfied under 37 CFR 1.312(b). If a patent issues without an election due to error (without deceptive intent), a reissue application may be filed to permit consideration. Reliance on 103(b) should be rare given Federal Circuit decisions (In re Ochiai; In re Brouwer). See MPEP § 2116.01 for related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary examination objective: focus on prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary object of the examination of an application is to determine whether or not the claims are patentable over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not relegate prior art consideration to a secondary position while giving undue emphasis to nonprior art or 'technical' rejections. Concentrate effort on truly essential matters; where a major technical rejection is proper (e.g., lack of proper disclosure, undue breadth, utility, etc.), state it with a full development of reasons rather than a mere conclusion or stereotyped expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use form paragraphs to state rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If the language in the form paragraphs is incorporated in the letter to state the rejection, there will be less chance of misunderstanding as to the grounds of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate form paragraphs (cited throughout these sections) for consistent, clear presentation of statutory rejections; precede certain rejections with the statutory form paragraph as required (e.g., 7.04 for first actions/final rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 101 statutory subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of the invention must come within the boundaries set forth by 35 U.S.C. 101, which permits patents only for 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.' The term 'process' as defined in 35 U.S.C. 100 means process, art or method, and includes a new use of a known process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claims define statutory subject matter; see related MPEP sections for patentability of microorganisms and algorithms (e.g., §§ 2105-2106.02). Use form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05 family where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of utility grounds under 35 U.S.C. 101
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection on the ground of lack of utility includes more specific grounds of inoperativeness, perpetual motion, frivolous, fraudulent, and against public policy. The statutory basis is 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the guidelines in MPEP § 706.03(a)(1) and legal precedent in §§ 2107-2107.02. Use form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05.02, 7.05.03) and provide explanation of lack of utility (frivolous, fraudulent, lack of chemical specificity, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of non-patentable subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of subject matter not patentable under the statute include 'printed matter' (mere arrangement of printed matter), 'naturally occurring article' (substantially unaltered things occurring in nature), and 'scientific principle' divorced from any tangible structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite appropriate precedent (e.g., In re Miller; Ex parte Gwinn; In re Jones; Ex parte Grayson; O'Reilly v. Morse) when rejecting as non-statutory subject matter. Use the Atomic Energy Act guidance where applicable for additional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.04 requirement in first actions
rubrics_metrics.description: ¶ 7.04 Statement of Statutory Basis, 35 U.S.C. 101 must precede the first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in all first actions on the merits and final rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph 7.04 (quotation of the statute) is required before first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions/final rejections; see Examiner Note that the statute may not be re-cited in all office actions, and where not cited use paragraph 7.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections (7.05 family)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific form paragraphs to present 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections: 7.05.01 (Non-Statutory), 7.05.02 (Utility Lacking), 7.05.03 (Inoperative), and 7.05.04 (Utility Rejections Under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112, First Paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In each form paragraph insert the required identification and explanation in the brackets per Examiner Notes. For utility/enablement interplay, use Wands factors and make a separate 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph enablement rejection where appropriate (see instructions in 7.05.04 and MPEP §§ 2164-2164.08(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility examination: determine what applicant has invented
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must determine what the applicant has invented and is seeking to patent by: (1) ensuring claims define statutory subject matter (process, machine, manufacture, composition), and (2) reviewing the complete specification including detailed description, embodiments, claims, and any asserted utilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough review of the entire disclosure and claims is required before assessing utility; do not rely on partial or isolated statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility examination: credible specific utility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant has asserted that the claimed invention is useful for a particular purpose (a 'specific utility') and that assertion would be considered credible by a person of ordinary skill in the art, do not impose a rejection based on lack of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility is assessed from the perspective of one of ordinary skill in the art in view of evidence of record (data, statements, opinions, references). An applicant must provide only one credible assertion of specific utility to satisfy the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility examination: well-established utility exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention has a well-established utility, regardless of any assertion made by the applicant, do not impose a rejection based on lack of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention has a well-established utility if a person of ordinary skill in the art would immediately appreciate why the invention is useful based on its characteristics (e.g., properties of a product or obvious application of a process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility examination: no asserted specific utility -> 101 and 112 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant has not asserted any specific utility for the claimed invention and it does not have a well-established utility, impose a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 (lack of utility) and a separate rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (failure to teach how to use the invention due to lack of disclosure of a specific utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 101 and 112 rejections should shift the burden to the applicant to (i) explicitly identify a specific utility for the claimed invention and (ii) indicate where support for the asserted utility can be found in the specification. Review subsequently asserted utilities under the credible-utility standard and ensure full support in the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing of no utility: required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify a rejection based on lack of utility, Office personnel must make a prima facie showing that it is more likely than not that a person skilled in the art would not consider credible any specific utility asserted by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper prima facie showing must include: (i) a well-reasoned statement clearly setting forth the reasoning used in concluding the asserted utility is not credible; (ii) support for factual findings relied upon; and (iii) support for conclusions regarding any evidence provided by the applicant. Provide documentary evidence (scientific/technical journals, treatises, patents) where possible; if documentary evidence is not available, note that and explain the scientific basis for factual conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility rejection: applicant rebuttal and examiner response
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a prima facie showing of no utility has been established, the applicant bears the burden of rebutting it by amending claims, providing reasoning/arguments, or providing evidence (declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 or a printed publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must review the original disclosure, evidence relied upon for the prima facie showing, claim amendments, and any new reasoning/evidence. Recognize, consider, and respond to each substantive element of any reply. Withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 101 and corresponding 112 rejections if the applicant satisfactorily rebuts the prima facie rejection. Treat as true a factual statement by applicant unless countervailing evidence provides legitimate basis to doubt credibility. Accept qualified expert opinions based on relevant facts unless the facts' accuracy is questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atomic Energy Act limitations and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: No patent shall be granted for any invention useful solely in the utilization of special nuclear material or atomic energy in an atomic weapon (Atomic Energy Act §151(a)). Sections 151(c)-(d) create categories of pending applications that must be reported to the Department of Energy. Applications that disclose or appear to disclose inventions relating to atomic energy are reported to the Department of Energy under 37 CFR 1.14(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group 3640 personnel screen all incoming applications under 37 CFR 1.14(c). Papers added later must be inspected promptly by the examiner to determine relation to atomic energy and forwarded to Licensing and Review in Group 3640. All rejections under sections 151(a), 152, and 155 of the Atomic Energy Act must be made only by Group 3640 personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph: written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ¶ 7.30.01 (statutory quotation) in first actions/final rejections. Use form paragraph 7.31.01 to reject when claimed subject matter was not described so as to reasonably convey that the inventor had possession at the filing date. In bracketed inserts identify by page/line/drawing where subject matter is missing and explain examiner's position, including unresolved examiner questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph: enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, if the specification does not enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention. (Form paragraph 7.31.02.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede this rejection with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Identify claimed subject matter not enabled and explain why the specification is not enabling, including any examiner questions not satisfactorily resolved. If the problem is scope-related, use form paragraph 7.31.03 instead. If an essential component or step is missing from the claims, use form paragraph 7.33.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph: scope of enablement (commensurateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected because the specification, while enabling for certain subject matter, does not reasonably provide enablement for other claimed aspects; the specification does not enable the invention commensurate in scope with the claims (form paragraph 7.31.03).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this when claim scope is broader than the enabling disclosure. Identify in bracketed inserts what is enabled (by reference) and which claim aspects are not enabled. Specify whether the deficiency is inability to 'make', 'use', or 'make and use', and explain why the specification is not enabling, including unresolved examiner queries.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph: best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected because the best mode contemplated by the inventor has not been disclosed (form paragraph 7.31.04).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103. In the rejection, insert the basis for holding that the best mode has been concealed (e.g., quality of disclosure so poor as to effectively result in concealment). Use this paragraph rarely; consult MPEP §§ 2165-2165.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph: essential subject matter missing from claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, as based on a disclosure which is not enabling because subject matter considered critical or essential to practice of the invention is omitted from the claims (form paragraph 7.33.01).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103. Recite omitted subject matter and give rationale for considering it critical or essential, citing statements/arguments/drawings or other evidence showing the applicant considered the feature essential but it is not reflected in the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph: failure to claim applicant's invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, for failing to set forth the subject matter which applicant(s) regard as their invention; evidence that a claim fails to correspond to applicant's stated invention can be shown in submissions (form paragraph 7.34).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103. Identify the applicant submission (paper number and date) and quote what applicant stated that indicates the invention is different from the claimed subject matter. Explain how the statement indicates a different invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph: indefiniteness (failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected as indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention (form paragraph 7.34.01).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103 and follow with specific form paragraphs (7.34.02-7.34.06) as applicable. Whenever possible identify particular term(s) or limitation(s) rendering the claim indefinite and explain why. If scope can be determined by one of ordinary skill, do not use this rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology used inconsistent with accepted meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A term in a claim may not be given a meaning repugnant to the usual meaning of that term; e.g., the term '[1]' used to mean '[3]' while accepted meaning is '[4]' (form paragraph 7.34.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only in aggravated situations where lack of antecedent basis makes scope indeterminate. Precede with 7.34.01. Support examiner's accepted meaning through citation of appropriate reference sources (textbook/dictionary) per MPEP § 2173.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative term / term of degree rendering claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A relative term (term of degree) in a claim can render the claim indefinite if the term is not defined by the claim and the specification provides no standard for ascertaining the requisite degree, so one of ordinary skill cannot be reasonably apprised of scope (form paragraph 7.34.03).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.34.01. In the rejection explain which parameter/quantity/limitation is rendered indefinite by the term and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad range and narrow range limitation in same claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad range or limitation together with a narrower range or limitation that falls within the broad range in the same claim is considered indefinite because the claim does not clearly set forth the metes and bounds of the protection desired (form paragraph 7.34.04).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the broader and narrower ranges/limitations and where they appear in the claim. Modify the paragraph to fit similar instances of indefiniteness and reference case law (e.g., Ex parte Wu). Precede with 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of antecedent basis in the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites a limitation with insufficient antecedent basis (e.g., using 'said lever' or 'the lever' without prior introduction) rendering the claim deficient (form paragraph 7.34.05).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the form paragraph insert the limitation lacking antecedent basis and where it appears. Precede with 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use claims that merely recite a use without steps are indefinite / improper process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that provides for the use of something but does not set forth any steps involved in the method/process is unclear what method/process is intended and is indefinite; such a claim may also be improper under 35 U.S.C. 101 as not a proper process claim (form paragraph 7.34.06).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert what is being used and explain the lack of active steps delimiting how use is practiced. Cite MPEP § 2173.05(q) and relevant decisions (Ex parte Dunki, Clinical Products v. Brenner). Precede with 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are literal translations (narrative/indefinite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are generally narrative and appear to be literal translations into English from a foreign document, with grammatical and idiomatic errors, are generally indefinite and fail to conform with current U.S. practice (form paragraph 7.34.07).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.34.01 and explain deficiencies. Recommend redrafting claims into standard U.S. claim format.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'For example' renders the claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the phrase 'for example' in a claim renders it indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention (form paragraph 7.34.08).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.34.01. Cite MPEP § 2173.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Or the like' renders the claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'or the like' renders a claim indefinite because it includes elements not actually disclosed, making the scope unascertainable (form paragraph 7.34.09).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.34.01 and cite MPEP § 2173.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Such as' renders the claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'such as' renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention (form paragraph 7.34.10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.34.01 and cite MPEP § 2173.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifier of 'means' lacks function (112, sixth paragraph issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the word 'means' is preceded by words that do not convey a function (e.g., 'conduit means'), it is impossible to determine equivalents as required by 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, rendering the claim indefinite (form paragraph 7.34.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.34.01. The words which precede 'means' must convey a function (e.g., 'latch means' conveys 'means for latching'). If the phrase cannot be restated as 'means for ________' sensibly, it is indefinite. Cite Ex parte Klumb and provide the necessary explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential steps omitted in method/process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential steps, the omission amounting to a gap between the recited steps (form paragraph 7.34.12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the omitted steps, explain why omission creates a gap between steps, and precede with 7.34.01. See MPEP § 2172.01 for reasoning.
